# People's Vanguard Party (Yemen)
The **People's Vanguard Party** (Arabic: حزب الطليعة الشعبية), also referred to as **at-Tali'a**,[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/People's_Vanguard_Party_(Yemen)#cite_note-1) was a [Ba'athist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ba'athism "Ba'athism") political party in Yemen.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/People's_Vanguard_Party_(Yemen)#cite_note-ta-2)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/People's_Vanguard_Party_(Yemen)#cite_note-3) The party was established in the late 1950s.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/People's_Vanguard_Party_(Yemen)#cite_note-nbr-4) It was the Yemeni branch of the Baath Party. When the Baath Party was divided between Syrian and Iraqi factions, the Yemeni branch overwhelmingly sided with the Syrian-led Ba'ath Party.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/People's_Vanguard_Party_(Yemen)#cite_note-hidi-5)[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/People's_Vanguard_Party_(Yemen)#cite_note-nbr-4)[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/People's_Vanguard_Party_(Yemen)#cite_note-6) After the split, the Syrian-aligned Ba'athists 'Yemenized' their party and took the name People's Vanguard Party.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/People's_Vanguard_Party_(Yemen)#cite_note-hidi-5)
[](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Conference_of_the_People's_Vanguard,_South_Yemen.jpg)
The Third Conference of the People's Vanguard Party

# People's Vanguard Party (Yemen)
The members of the party were largely recruited from teachers, students, and intellectuals.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/People's_Vanguard_Party_(Yemen)#cite_note-nbr-4) The party was based in Aden, and had limited presence outside the city.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/People's_Vanguard_Party_(Yemen)#cite_note-nbr-4) It had some presence in Hadhramaut for a brief period.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/People's_Vanguard_Party_(Yemen)#cite_note-nbr-4) The party was banned in North Yemen, where it was part of the National Democratic Front and took part in the NDF Rebellion.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/People's_Vanguard_Party_(Yemen)#cite_note-hidi-5)
The party was one of two non-National Front (NF) parties tolerated during the early 1970s. In October 1975 it joined the NF-dominated United Political Organization of the National Front[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/People's_Vanguard_Party_(Yemen)#cite_note-Hobday-7) (which evolved into the Yemeni Socialist Party in 1978).[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/People's_Vanguard_Party_(Yemen)#cite_note-ta-2) The merger was ratified by the third PVP congress held in August 1975.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/People's_Vanguard_Party_(Yemen)#cite_note-8)

The Vanguard provides the Davis Community with incisive in-depth coverage of local government on a wide variety of issues. Since 2006, The Vanguard has provided Davis and Yolo County with some of the best groundbreaking news coverage on local government and policy issues affecting our city, our schools, the county, and the Sacramento Region. Our organization became a 501(c)(3) non-profit in 2012.

## Mission
The People's Vanguard of Davis is a community-based watchdog and news reporting organization that publishes daily coverage of local government and criminal justice reform. The Vanguard seeks to bring transparency, accountability, and fairness to local government and the courts, while promoting social justice and democracy, and adhering to principles of accuracy and fairness in our reporting.

## Needs
The Vanguard Court Watch program is dedicated to reporting and monitoring court cases. This program has allowed interns the opportunity to publish articles, watch live court cases, and learn about the criminal justice system and local reporting.
The Davis Vanguard currently hosts a Court Watch Program in 3 branches: Yolo County, Sacramento County, and San Francisco County. Our funding ranges from office space and supplies to website expenses. Your contributions will help in keeping the court proceedings transparent and accountable.
We expanded our Court Watch Program to San Francisco in June 2019 and are considering expanding our program further into other California counties, such as Los Angeles.
In addition to our Court Watch Program, our organization needs funds in order to host fundraiser events relating to criminal justice reform. Among the topics we've held events, we've addressed the need to reform the prosecution system and immigration. During these events, we invite guest speakers from all across the country.
The Davis Vanguard at UC Davis is a student-run online news publication presenting campus news, city news, social justice issues, and student opinions. Students interested in writing for the Davis Vanguard at UCD will have the opportunity to develop a strong journalistic portfolio, gain experience with community outreach, training with an experienced Sacramento journalist, and earn academic credit.
Any donations are appreciated in supporting our organization.

## Equity Statement
The People’s Vanguard of Davis is committed to transparent journalism, driving reform, amplifying voices, and exposing systemic injustices, particularly those affecting marginalized communities. Through our investigative journalism, Court Watch program, and Vanguard Incarcerated Press, we aim to serve those often neglected or mistreated in our judicial system and mainstream media. This includes members of the BIPOC community, the LGBTQ+ community, individuals with disabilities, the unhoused, and those who are economically disadvantaged.

## Programs and results
### Our programs
#### The Vanguard Incarcerated Press (VIP
The Vanguard Incarcerated Press (VIP) is a journalism training and publishing program for incarcerated individuals in California. VIP equips participants with writing and reporting skills while offering a platform to share their stories, highlight prison conditions, and expose systemic injustices. The program fosters personal growth, civic engagement, and healing through self-expression. VIP primarily serves incarcerated people from marginalized communities—especially BIPOC and LGBTQ+ individuals—who often lack access to educational and rehabilitative resources. By amplifying their voices, VIP challenges public perceptions and support justice reform. We currently serve 180 individuals and are expanding to reach 360 by June 2025.

### Our programs
#### The Court Watch Program
The Court Watch Program promotes transparency and accountability in the justice system by training interns and volunteers to observe, document, and report on court proceedings. We focus on cases involving marginalized individuals, where judicial bias and misconduct often go unchecked. Our trained observers attend hearings, take detailed notes, and publish reports that highlight systemic issues. These insights are shared with the public, media, and reform advocates to inform policy change. Through civic engagement and legal education, Court Watch empowers communities to hold courts accountable and work toward a fairer, more equitable legal system.

### Our programs
#### The Vanguard's Investigative Journalism Project
We conduct deep investigations into wrongful convictions, police violence, and abuse in jails and prisons, using legal research, FOIA requests, and expert analysis. Our team also delivers rapid coverage of unfolding court cases, protests, and policy developments, ensuring timely scrutiny of emerging issues. We prioritize the voices of those directly impacted—featuring first-person narratives, interviews with families of the incarcerated, and grassroots advocates. Our work extends beyond reporting through public forums and community workshops that foster dialogue and awareness. We also collaborate with advocacy groups, universities, and media partners to broaden impact and support reform efforts.

# People's Vanguard Party (Yemen)
The **People's Vanguard Party** (Arabic: حزب الطليعة الشعبية), also referred to as **at-Tali'a**,[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/People's_Vanguard_Party_(Yemen)#cite_note-1) was a [Ba'athist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ba'athism "Ba'athism") political party in Yemen.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/People's_Vanguard_Party_(Yemen)#cite_note-ta-2)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/People's_Vanguard_Party_(Yemen)#cite_note-3) The party was established in the late 1950s.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/People's_Vanguard_Party_(Yemen)#cite_note-nbr-4) It was the Yemeni branch of the Baath Party. When the Baath Party was divided between Syrian and Iraqi factions, the Yemeni branch overwhelmingly sided with the Syrian-led Ba'ath Party.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/People's_Vanguard_Party_(Yemen)#cite_note-hidi-5)[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/People's_Vanguard_Party_(Yemen)#cite_note-nbr-4)[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/People's_Vanguard_Party_(Yemen)#cite_note-6) After the split, the Syrian-aligned Ba'athists 'Yemenized' their party and took the name People's Vanguard Party.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/People's_Vanguard_Party_(Yemen)#cite_note-hidi-5)
[](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Conference_of_the_People's_Vanguard,_South_Yemen.jpg)
The Third Conference of the People's Vanguard Party
texts.5:
# People's Vanguard Party (Yemen)
The members of the party were largely recruited from teachers, students, and intellectuals.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/People's_Vanguard_Party_(Yemen)#cite_note-nbr-4) The party was based in Aden, and had limited presence outside the city.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/People's_Vanguard_Party_(Yemen)#cite_note-nbr-4) It had some presence in Hadhramaut for a brief period.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/People's_Vanguard_Party_(Yemen)#cite_note-nbr-4) The party was banned in North Yemen, where it was part of the National Democratic Front and took part in the NDF Rebellion.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/People's_Vanguard_Party_(Yemen)#cite_note-hidi-5)
The party was one of two non-National Front (NF) parties tolerated during the early 1970s. In October 1975 it joined the NF-dominated United Political Organization of the National Front[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/People's_Vanguard_Party_(Yemen)#cite_note-Hobday-7) (which evolved into the Yemeni Socialist Party in 1978).[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/People's_Vanguard_Party_(Yemen)#cite_note-ta-2) The merger was ratified by the third PVP congress held in August 1975.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/People's_Vanguard_Party_(Yemen)#cite_note-8)

## Mission
The People's Vanguard of Davis is a community-based watchdog and news reporting organization that publishes daily coverage of local government and criminal justice reform. The Vanguard seeks to bring transparency, accountability, and fairness to local government and the courts, while promoting social justice and democracy, and adhering to principles of accuracy and fairness in our reporting.
texts.2:
## Needs
The Vanguard Court Watch program is dedicated to reporting and monitoring court cases. This program has allowed interns the opportunity to publish articles, watch live court cases, and learn about the criminal justice system and local reporting.
The Davis Vanguard currently hosts a Court Watch Program in 3 branches: Yolo County, Sacramento County, and San Francisco County. Our funding ranges from office space and supplies to website expenses. Your contributions will help in keeping the court proceedings transparent and accountable.
We expanded our Court Watch Program to San Francisco in June 2019 and are considering expanding our program further into other California counties, such as Los Angeles.
In addition to our Court Watch Program, our organization needs funds in order to host fundraiser events relating to criminal justice reform. Among the topics we've held events, we've addressed the need to reform the prosecution system and immigration. During these events, we invite guest speakers from all across the country.
The Davis Vanguard at UC Davis is a student-run online news publication presenting campus news, city news, social justice issues, and student opinions. Students interested in writing for the Davis Vanguard at UCD will have the opportunity to develop a strong journalistic portfolio, gain experience with community outreach, training with an experienced Sacramento journalist, and earn academic credit.
Any donations are appreciated in supporting our organization.
texts.3:
## Equity Statement
The People’s Vanguard of Davis is committed to transparent journalism, driving reform, amplifying voices, and exposing systemic injustices, particularly those affecting marginalized communities. Through our investigative journalism, Court Watch program, and Vanguard Incarcerated Press, we aim to serve those often neglected or mistreated in our judicial system and mainstream media. This includes members of the BIPOC community, the LGBTQ+ community, individuals with disabilities, the unhoused, and those who are economically disadvantaged.

#### The Vanguard Incarcerated Press (VIP
The Vanguard Incarcerated Press (VIP) is a journalism training and publishing program for incarcerated individuals in California. VIP equips participants with writing and reporting skills while offering a platform to share their stories, highlight prison conditions, and expose systemic injustices. The program fosters personal growth, civic engagement, and healing through self-expression. VIP primarily serves incarcerated people from marginalized communities—especially BIPOC and LGBTQ+ individuals—who often lack access to educational and rehabilitative resources. By amplifying their voices, VIP challenges public perceptions and support justice reform. We currently serve 180 individuals and are expanding to reach 360 by June 2025.

# People's Vanguard Party (Yemen)
The **People's Vanguard Party** (Arabic: حزب الطليعة الشعبية), also referred to as **at-Tali'a**,[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/People's_Vanguard_Party_(Yemen)#cite_note-1) was a [Ba'athist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ba'athism "Ba'athism") political party in Yemen.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/People's_Vanguard_Party_(Yemen)#cite_note-ta-2)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/People's_Vanguard_Party_(Yemen)#cite_note-3) The party was established in the late 1950s.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/People's_Vanguard_Party_(Yemen)#cite_note-nbr-4) It was the Yemeni branch of the Baath Party. When the Baath Party was divided between Syrian and Iraqi factions, the Yemeni branch overwhelmingly sided with the Syrian-led Ba'ath Party.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/People's_Vanguard_Party_(Yemen)#cite_note-hidi-5)[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/People's_Vanguard_Party_(Yemen)#cite_note-nbr-4)[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/People's_Vanguard_Party_(Yemen)#cite_note-6) After the split, the Syrian-aligned Ba'athists 'Yemenized' their party and took the name People's Vanguard Party.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/People's_Vanguard_Party_(Yemen)#cite_note-hidi-5)
[](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Conference_of_the_People's_Vanguard,_South_Yemen.jpg)
The Third Conference of the People's Vanguard Party

# People's Vanguard Party (Yemen)
The members of the party were largely recruited from teachers, students, and intellectuals.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/People's_Vanguard_Party_(Yemen)#cite_note-nbr-4) The party was based in Aden, and had limited presence outside the city.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/People's_Vanguard_Party_(Yemen)#cite_note-nbr-4) It had some presence in Hadhramaut for a brief period.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/People's_Vanguard_Party_(Yemen)#cite_note-nbr-4) The party was banned in North Yemen, where it was part of the National Democratic Front and took part in the NDF Rebellion.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/People's_Vanguard_Party_(Yemen)#cite_note-hidi-5)
The party was one of two non-National Front (NF) parties tolerated during the early 1970s. In October 1975 it joined the NF-dominated United Political Organization of the National Front[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/People's_Vanguard_Party_(Yemen)#cite_note-Hobday-7) (which evolved into the Yemeni Socialist Party in 1978).[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/People's_Vanguard_Party_(Yemen)#cite_note-ta-2) The merger was ratified by the third PVP congress held in August 1975.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/People's_Vanguard_Party_(Yemen)#cite_note-8)

The **Aden Emergency**, also known as the **14 October Revolution**[[a]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aden_Emergency#cite_note-8) or the **Aden Insurgency**, was an armed rebellion led mainly by the National Liberation Front (NLF) and the Front for the Liberation of Occupied South Yemen (FLOSY) against the British Protectorate and Federation of South Arabia. It began on 14 October 1963 when tribes from Radfan attacked British troops and ended with the proclamation of independence of the [People's Republic of Southern Yemen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/People's_Republic_of_Southern_Yemen "People's Republic of Southern Yemen").

The British had declared a state of emergency following the throwing of a grenade at a gathering of British officials on 10 December 1963 at RAF Khormaksar. A state of emergency was then declared in the British Crown colony of Aden and its hinterland, the Aden Protectorate. The emergency escalated in 1967, which hastened the end of British rule in the territory, which had begun in 1839.

### British arrival in Yemen
[edit]
The first political intercourse between Yemen and the British took place in 1799 during the French invasion of Egypt and Syria, when a naval force was sent from Britain, with a detachment of troops from India, to occupy the island of Perim and prevent all communication of the French in Egypt with the Indian Ocean, by way of the Red Sea. Due to the lack of water supply, the barren and inhospitable island of Perim was found unsuitable for troops.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aden_Emergency#cite_note-9)[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aden_Emergency#cite_note-10) The Sultan of Lahej, Ahmed bin Abdul Karim, then received the detachment for some time at Aden. He proposed to enter into an alliance and to grant Aden as a permanent station, but the offer was declined. A treaty was, however, concluded with the Sultan in 1802 by Admiral Home Popham, who was instructed to enter into political and commercial alliances with the Chiefs of the Arabian coast of the Red Sea.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aden_Emergency#cite_note-:0-11)

### British arrival in Yemen
By the early 1800s, the British were looking for a coaling station to fuel their steamships through their journey from the Suez Canal to the British Raj.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aden_Emergency#cite_note-FOOTNOTEClark201029-12) The British tried to negotiate with the Mahra Sultanate to buy the island of Socotra, located in the Arabian Sea, but the Sultan of Mahra refused and told the British naval officer who was tasked with the mission that the island was "the gift of the Almighty to the Mahris".[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aden_Emergency#cite_note-FOOTNOTEClark201029-12)[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aden_Emergency#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBijl20144-13) In 1835, a year after the British had given up on Socotra, they had attempted to purchase the port city of Aden and its inlet from the Sultan of Lahej, Muhsin Bin Fadl, but they failed. In 1837, the _Duria Dawla_, an Indian ship flying the Union Jack, crashed near the east coast of Aden and was looted by local tribesmen. A year after the incident, in 1838, British officials arrived in Lahej and demanded 12,000 Maria Theresa thalers (MTT) as compensation for the losses. The sultan, unable to pay that sum of money, was forced to cede Aden to the British for a sum of 8,700 MTT a year.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aden_Emergency#cite_note-FOOTNOTEClark201031-14) On 19 January 1839, the British East India Company landed Royal Marines at Aden to retain full control of Aden and stop attacks by pirates against British shipping to India.

### Beginning of end of British rule in Yemen
The FSA did not succeed for several reasons, the first of which was the British insistence that the State of Aden would be part of the entity, which was rejected by the commercial elite of Aden, most of which was Indians, Persians and Jews, because it feared that Aden's wealth would be taken away by the neighbouring sheikhdoms.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aden_Emergency#cite_note-Online._Encyclop%C3%A6dia_Britannica_Inc_2013-15)[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aden_Emergency#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDay201238-20)[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aden_Emergency#cite_note-FOOTNOTEStookey198255-21) On the other hand, the leaders of the sheikhdoms had little experience with federal rule and had no desire for cooperation.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aden_Emergency#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDay201239-16) In addition, there were differences between the sheikhdoms over who should head the federation's new government.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aden_Emergency#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDay201239-16)

### Beginning of end of British rule in Yemen
In 26 September 1962, a successful coup carried out against the Kingdom of Yemen by the Free Officers Movement in Yemen[ar], supported by Egyptian President Gamal Abdel Nasser, who had led the Egyptian Revolution of 1952 against British rule, resulted in the establishment of the Yemen Arab Republic.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aden_Emergency#cite_note-FOOTNOTEClark201062%E2%80%9365-22)[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aden_Emergency#cite_note-sandler977-23) This coup inspired organisations, such as the local branch of the Movement of Arab Nationalists and the Aden Trade Union Congress, to form the National Liberation Front (NLF)[[b]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aden_Emergency#cite_note-24) and the Front for the Liberation of Occupied South Yemen (FLOSY),[[c]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aden_Emergency#cite_note-25) respectively.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aden_Emergency#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBarany20167-26)[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aden_Emergency#cite_note-FOOTNOTEClark201076-27) Supporters of the NLF were from the countryside of Radfan, [Yafa'](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yafa'a "Yafa'a"), and Ad-Dali, while the supporters of the FLOSY were mainly the citizens of Aden because tribal affiliations played a major role in attracting supporters.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aden_Emergency#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMumford201487-28)

### Involved organisations
[edit]
There were a number of different nationalist groups fighting the British, which often fought one another. The most well-known groups are:[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aden_Emergency#cite_note-autogenerated2-5)
1.   The National Liberation Front (NLF)  
2.   The Front for the Liberation of South Yemen (FLOSY)  
3.   The South Arabian League (SAL)  
4.   The Organization for the Liberation of the Occupied South (OLOS)  
5.   The [People's Socialist Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/People's_Socialist_Party_(Yemen)?action=edit&redlink=1 "People's Socialist Party (Yemen) (page does not exist)") (PLP)[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aden_Emergency#cite_note-FOOTNOTENaumkin200450-29)
Among the main players, the SAL was backed by Saudi Arabia, the FLOSY by Egypt and the Aden Trade Unions. All of the major groups were based in Yemen, and they regularly combined and split with other groups. For instance, SAL joined with PSP to become OLOS in 1965, and then broke away in 1966. The NLF joined with OLOS in January 1966 to form FLOSY but broke away in December 1966. Such movements were quite common throughout the war.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aden_Emergency#cite_note-:0-11)

### Grenade attack and British declaration of state of emergency
[edit]
The British declared a state of emergency on 10 December 1963, following an NLF grenade attack on the British High Commissioner of Aden, Sir Kennedy Trevaskis, which took place as he arrived at Khormaksar Airport to catch a London-bound flight. The grenade killed the High Commissioner's adviser and a woman and injured fifty other people.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aden_Emergency#cite_note-30)
NLF and FLOSY began a campaign against British forces in Aden that relied largely on grenade attacks. One such attack was carried out against RAF Khormaksar during a [children's party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Children's_Party_attack "Children's Party attack"), killing a girl and wounding four children.
The guerrilla attacks largely focused on killing off-duty British officers and policemen. Much of the violence was carried out in Crater, the old Arab quarter of Aden. British forces attempted to intercept weapons being smuggled into Crater by the NLF and FLOSY on the Dhala road, but their efforts met with little success. Despite taking a toll on British forces, the death toll among rebels was far higher, largely because of interfactional fighting among different rebel groups.
Aden in 1965
NLF graffiti in Mansoura, 1966: "No freedom without blood"
By 1965, the RAF station RAF Khormaksar was operating nine squadrons, including transport units with helicopters and several Hawker Hunter fighter-bomber aircraft. The army called in these for attacks on rebel positions in which they would use 60-pound high explosive rockets and their 30 mm ADEN cannon.
Street riots in Aden, 1967
Aden in 1967

### Grenade attack and British declaration of state of emergency
On 19–20 January 1967, the NLF provoked street riots in Aden. After the Aden police lost control, British High Commissioner Sir Richard Turnbull deployed British troops to crush the riots. As soon as the NLF riots were crushed, pro-FLOSY rioters took to the streets. Fighting between British forces and pro-guerrilla rioters lasted into February. British forces opened fire 40 times, and during that period there were 60 grenade and shooting attacks against British forces, including the destruction of an Aden AirwaysDouglas DC-3, which was bombed in mid-air, killing all the people on board.
At one point, toward the end of the rebellion in early 1967 the NLF killed at least 35 members of FLOSY in 32 days. The FLOSY guerrillas first asked the British for protection, and then 80 actually flew to the UK using the British passports they had as citizens of a British Colony.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aden_Emergency#cite_note-:0-11)
The emergency was further exacerbated by the Six-Day War in June 1967. Egyptian President Gamal Abdel Nasser claimed that the British had helped Israel in the war, which led to a mutiny by hundreds of soldiers in the South Arabian Federation Army on June 20 that spread to the Aden Armed Police. The mutineers killed 22 British soldiers and shot down a helicopter. The pilot had to abandon a takeoff from a ledge near Crater after being hit in the knee by a bullet. The Sioux helicopter crashed and burned out, but all three occupants escaped. As a result, Crater was occupied by rebel forces.
Concerns were heightened regarding the ability to give sufficient security to British families in the midst of the increased violence, resulting in evacuation plans for families being sped up considerably.

### Grenade attack and British declaration of state of emergency
Following the mutiny, all British forces were withdrawn from Crater, and Royal Marines of 45 Commando took up sniping positions on the high ground and killed 10 armed Arab fighters. However, Crater remained occupied by an estimated 400 Arab fighters. NLF and FLOSY fighters then took to the streets and engaged in gun battles, and arson, looting and murder were also common. British forces blocked off the two main entrances to Crater. They came under sniper fire from an Ottoman fort on Sira Island, but the snipers were silenced by a shell from an armoured car. Order was restored in July 1967, when the 1st Argyll and Sutherland Highlanders entered Crater under the command of Lt. Col.Colin Campbell Mitchell and managed to occupy the entire district overnight with no casualties.

### British withdrawal from Yemen
[edit]
NLF supporters waving their flags as part of the celebrations and mass marches on 29 and 30 November, 1967
Lowering of the Union Flag in Aden
Nevertheless, repeated guerrilla attacks by the NLF soon resumed against British forces, causing the British to leave Aden by the end of November 1967, earlier than had been planned by British Prime Minister Harold Wilson and without an agreement on the succeeding governance. That effectively abandoned the South Arabian government.
On 30 November 1967, the _Federation of South Arabia_ ceased to exist when the [People's Republic of Southern Yemen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/People's_Republic_of_Southern_Yemen "People's Republic of Southern Yemen") was proclaimed. In 1967, Israel defeated Egypt in the Six-Day War, thus obliging Egypt to evacuate its troops from Yemen. FLOSY, now without any military support from its Egyptian ally, continued fighting the NLF. However, FLOSY's fate was sealed when the NLF managed to persuade the Yemen Federal Army to join the fight. On 7 November 1967, FLOSY tried to attack a federal army base, but the army defeated FLOSY with the NLF's help, inflicting heavy losses on FLOSY. After the defeat, FLOSY's fighting force disbanded although some cadres and leaders remained outside the country.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aden_Emergency#cite_note-31) Most of the opposing leaders reconciled by 1968, in the aftermath of a final royalist siege of San'a'.
British military casualties from 1963 to 1967 were 90 to 92 killed[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aden_Emergency#cite_note-32) and 510 wounded. British civilian deaths were 17. Local government forces lost 17 killed and 58 wounded. Casualties among the rebel forces stood at 382 killed and 1,714 wounded.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aden_Emergency#cite_note-autogenerated1-6)[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aden_Emergency#cite_note-autogenerated2-5)

In 26 September 1962, a successful coup carried out against the Kingdom of Yemen by the Free Officers Movement in Yemen[ar], supported by Egyptian President Gamal Abdel Nasser, who had led the Egyptian Revolution of 1952 against British rule, resulted in the establishment of the Yemen Arab Republic.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aden_Emergency#cite_note-FOOTNOTEClark201062%E2%80%9365-22)[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aden_Emergency#cite_note-sandler977-23) This coup inspired organisations, such as the local branch of the Movement of Arab Nationalists and the Aden Trade Union Congress, to form the National Liberation Front (NLF)[[b]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aden_Emergency#cite_note-24) and the Front for the Liberation of Occupied South Yemen (FLOSY),[[c]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aden_Emergency#cite_note-25) respectively.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aden_Emergency#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBarany20167-26)[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aden_Emergency#cite_note-FOOTNOTEClark201076-27) Supporters of the NLF were from the countryside of Radfan, [Yafa'](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yafa'a "Yafa'a"), and Ad-Dali, while the supporters of the FLOSY were mainly the citizens of Aden because tribal affiliations played a major role in attracting supporters.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aden_Emergency#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMumford201487-28)

### Involved organisations
[edit]
There were a number of different nationalist groups fighting the British, which often fought one another. The most well-known groups are:[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aden_Emergency#cite_note-autogenerated2-5)
1.   The National Liberation Front (NLF)  
2.   The Front for the Liberation of South Yemen (FLOSY)  
3.   The South Arabian League (SAL)  
4.   The Organization for the Liberation of the Occupied South (OLOS)  
5.   The [People's Socialist Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/People's_Socialist_Party_(Yemen)?action=edit&redlink=1 "People's Socialist Party (Yemen) (page does not exist)") (PLP)[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aden_Emergency#cite_note-FOOTNOTENaumkin200450-29)
Among the main players, the SAL was backed by Saudi Arabia, the FLOSY by Egypt and the Aden Trade Unions. All of the major groups were based in Yemen, and they regularly combined and split with other groups. For instance, SAL joined with PSP to become OLOS in 1965, and then broke away in 1966. The NLF joined with OLOS in January 1966 to form FLOSY but broke away in December 1966. Such movements were quite common throughout the war.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aden_Emergency#cite_note-:0-11)

### Grenade attack and British declaration of state of emergency
[edit]
The British declared a state of emergency on 10 December 1963, following an NLF grenade attack on the British High Commissioner of Aden, Sir Kennedy Trevaskis, which took place as he arrived at Khormaksar Airport to catch a London-bound flight. The grenade killed the High Commissioner's adviser and a woman and injured fifty other people.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aden_Emergency#cite_note-30)
NLF and FLOSY began a campaign against British forces in Aden that relied largely on grenade attacks. One such attack was carried out against RAF Khormaksar during a [children's party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Children's_Party_attack "Children's Party attack"), killing a girl and wounding four children.
The guerrilla attacks largely focused on killing off-duty British officers and policemen. Much of the violence was carried out in Crater, the old Arab quarter of Aden. British forces attempted to intercept weapons being smuggled into Crater by the NLF and FLOSY on the Dhala road, but their efforts met with little success. Despite taking a toll on British forces, the death toll among rebels was far higher, largely because of interfactional fighting among different rebel groups.
Aden in 1965
NLF graffiti in Mansoura, 1966: "No freedom without blood"
By 1965, the RAF station RAF Khormaksar was operating nine squadrons, including transport units with helicopters and several Hawker Hunter fighter-bomber aircraft. The army called in these for attacks on rebel positions in which they would use 60-pound high explosive rockets and their 30 mm ADEN cannon.

texts.13:
### Grenade attack and British declaration of state of emergency
On 19–20 January 1967, the NLF provoked street riots in Aden. After the Aden police lost control, British High Commissioner Sir Richard Turnbull deployed British troops to crush the riots. As soon as the NLF riots were crushed, pro-FLOSY rioters took to the streets. Fighting between British forces and pro-guerrilla rioters lasted into February. British forces opened fire 40 times, and during that period there were 60 grenade and shooting attacks against British forces, including the destruction of an Aden AirwaysDouglas DC-3, which was bombed in mid-air, killing all the people on board.
At one point, toward the end of the rebellion in early 1967 the NLF killed at least 35 members of FLOSY in 32 days. The FLOSY guerrillas first asked the British for protection, and then 80 actually flew to the UK using the British passports they had as citizens of a British Colony.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aden_Emergency#cite_note-:0-11)
The emergency was further exacerbated by the Six-Day War in June 1967. Egyptian President Gamal Abdel Nasser claimed that the British had helped Israel in the war, which led to a mutiny by hundreds of soldiers in the South Arabian Federation Army on June 20 that spread to the Aden Armed Police. The mutineers killed 22 British soldiers and shot down a helicopter. The pilot had to abandon a takeoff from a ledge near Crater after being hit in the knee by a bullet. The Sioux helicopter crashed and burned out, but all three occupants escaped. As a result, Crater was occupied by rebel forces.
Concerns were heightened regarding the ability to give sufficient security to British families in the midst of the increased violence, resulting in evacuation plans for families being sped up considerably.
texts.14:
### Grenade attack and British declaration of state of emergency
Following the mutiny, all British forces were withdrawn from Crater, and Royal Marines of 45 Commando took up sniping positions on the high ground and killed 10 armed Arab fighters. However, Crater remained occupied by an estimated 400 Arab fighters. NLF and FLOSY fighters then took to the streets and engaged in gun battles, and arson, looting and murder were also common. British forces blocked off the two main entrances to Crater. They came under sniper fire from an Ottoman fort on Sira Island, but the snipers were silenced by a shell from an armoured car. Order was restored in July 1967, when the 1st Argyll and Sutherland Highlanders entered Crater under the command of Lt. Col.Colin Campbell Mitchell and managed to occupy the entire district overnight with no casualties.
texts.15:
### British withdrawal from Yemen
[edit]
NLF supporters waving their flags as part of the celebrations and mass marches on 29 and 30 November, 1967
Lowering of the Union Flag in Aden
Nevertheless, repeated guerrilla attacks by the NLF soon resumed against British forces, causing the British to leave Aden by the end of November 1967, earlier than had been planned by British Prime Minister Harold Wilson and without an agreement on the succeeding governance. That effectively abandoned the South Arabian government.
On 30 November 1967, the _Federation of South Arabia_ ceased to exist when the [People's Republic of Southern Yemen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/People's_Republic_of_Southern_Yemen "People's Republic of Southern Yemen") was proclaimed. In 1967, Israel defeated Egypt in the Six-Day War, thus obliging Egypt to evacuate its troops from Yemen. FLOSY, now without any military support from its Egyptian ally, continued fighting the NLF. However, FLOSY's fate was sealed when the NLF managed to persuade the Yemen Federal Army to join the fight. On 7 November 1967, FLOSY tried to attack a federal army base, but the army defeated FLOSY with the NLF's help, inflicting heavy losses on FLOSY. After the defeat, FLOSY's fighting force disbanded although some cadres and leaders remained outside the country.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aden_Emergency#cite_note-31) Most of the opposing leaders reconciled by 1968, in the aftermath of a final royalist siege of San'a'.
British military casualties from 1963 to 1967 were 90 to 92 killed[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aden_Emergency#cite_note-32) and 510 wounded. British civilian deaths were 17. Local government forces lost 17 killed and 58 wounded. Casualties among the rebel forces stood at 382 killed and 1,714 wounded.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aden_Emergency#cite_note-autogenerated1-6)[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aden_Emergency#cite_note-autogenerated2-5)

The **Aden Emergency**, also known as the **14 October Revolution**[[a]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aden_Emergency#cite_note-8) or the **Aden Insurgency**, was an armed rebellion led mainly by the National Liberation Front (NLF) and the Front for the Liberation of Occupied South Yemen (FLOSY) against the British Protectorate and Federation of South Arabia. It began on 14 October 1963 when tribes from Radfan attacked British troops and ended with the proclamation of independence of the [People's Republic of Southern Yemen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/People's_Republic_of_Southern_Yemen "People's Republic of Southern Yemen").

The British had declared a state of emergency following the throwing of a grenade at a gathering of British officials on 10 December 1963 at RAF Khormaksar. A state of emergency was then declared in the British Crown colony of Aden and its hinterland, the Aden Protectorate. The emergency escalated in 1967, which hastened the end of British rule in the territory, which had begun in 1839.

[edit]
The first political intercourse between Yemen and the British took place in 1799 during the French invasion of Egypt and Syria, when a naval force was sent from Britain, with a detachment of troops from India, to occupy the island of Perim and prevent all communication of the French in Egypt with the Indian Ocean, by way of the Red Sea. Due to the lack of water supply, the barren and inhospitable island of Perim was found unsuitable for troops.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aden_Emergency#cite_note-9)[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aden_Emergency#cite_note-10) The Sultan of Lahej, Ahmed bin Abdul Karim, then received the detachment for some time at Aden.
